name: Deno
summary: A JavaScript and TypeScript runtime that combines standard module graphs with explicit, resource-scoped permission checks and worker construction carrying permission state.

features.name: Explicit resource-scoped permissions
features.description: Deno mediates sensitive resource classes such as read, write, net, env, run, ffi, and import through permission descriptors. Permissions can be queried, requested, revoked, and scoped by path, host, command, or variable.
benefits: Makes host resource authority explicit at runtime
Allows narrower grants than an unrestricted process environment
costs: Code must handle denied or partial permissions
FFI and subprocess permissions can cross the runtime's ordinary mediation boundary

features.name: Standard module graph with runtime imports
features.description: Deno uses ECMAScript modules as its primary module system, loads statically analyzable imports as part of the module graph, and checks computed dynamic imports against relevant permissions at runtime. It also supports CommonJS interoperability.
benefits: Preserves browser-compatible import and export structure
Separates graph loading from later resource operations
costs: Static and computed imports have different permission behavior
Interoperability adds resolution and evaluation cases

features.name: Permission-carrying worker construction
features.description: The fixed Deno source passes a root PermissionsContainer into main-worker construction and accepts a PermissionsContainer for custom worker creation, making permission state an explicit input to runtime worker setup.
benefits: Makes authority part of worker lifecycle construction
Provides a boundary for applying different worker execution modes
costs: Worker creation must coordinate execution configuration with permission state
The card does not establish a complete worker inheritance or restriction policy

mathematical_views.question: How do permission descriptors and permission transitions constrain resource operations during runtime execution?
assumptions: A permission descriptor is modeled as a capability predicate over a resource
Query, request, revoke, and operation transitions consult the current permission state
The model abstracts OS-level enforcement and the full permission broker protocol

mathematical_views.question: Which module-loading transitions are graph construction and which require a runtime permission decision?
assumptions: Modules are graph nodes and import edges carry static or computed resolution labels
Statically analyzable edges are loaded during graph construction
Computed edges are evaluated as runtime transitions subject to permission checks

costs: Permission failures and bypass-capable privileges require handling
Static versus computed import semantics differ

benefits: Worker setup has an explicit authority input
costs: Worker lifecycle configuration becomes more coupled
